note: Proposes phased evaluation by analogy to drug trials, which gives an audit a maturity scale to place a deployment on.
title: Evaluating artificial intelligence in medicine: phases of clinical research

reading.body:
A 2020 paper argues that healthcare AI should be evaluated in stages, like drug trials, because a good technical test result does not prove a tool works in real care.

The proposed framework maps AI evaluation onto the phases used for medicines and devices, and offers study design guidance for each stage. The reasoning is that healthcare is complex and AI performance depends on the people and setting using it, so laboratory or computer based testing alone is insufficient. The output is a maturity scale: a deployment can be placed at a stage, and the evidence expected of it can be set accordingly.

For AI specifically, this reframes what counts as proof. A model that performs well in a controlled technical test has cleared only an early hurdle, and the later hurdles concern context, users, and real settings rather than the model alone. That matters for governance and procurement, because it gives decision makers a basis for asking whether the evidence offered matches the stage a tool has actually reached, and for deciding when to pilot, expand, audit, or pause.

The data covers the framework and its reception, not its use. It records 128 citations and a publication year of 2020, and nothing here shows whether health systems, regulators, or vendors have adopted staged evaluation in practice, or how any specific deployment scored on the scale. The paper is also specific to medicine, so it does not establish how evaluation should work in other domains.

explain_beginner: This paper suggests that artificial intelligence used in healthcare should be checked in stages, much like new medicines are tested step by step. The authors say laboratory only testing is not enough because healthcare is complicated and AI tools can behave differently depending on the people and setting using them. They propose a shared, staged approach that combines different fields and gives guidance for what to study at each point. This matters because it offers a clearer way to judge whether an AI tool is useful and safe in real care, and it can help track how mature a deployment is.
explain_business: For executives, this paper says healthcare AI should be judged through staged evidence, similar to how drugs move through trials. A strong result in a controlled technical test is not enough. The framework helps leaders decide when to pilot, expand, audit, or pause an AI deployment. It also offers a maturity scale for placing a deployment, so decision makers can compare tools and set expectations for proof at each stage. In practice, this informs governance, procurement, and rollout choices, because it encourages asking for evidence that matches the tool's real setting, users, and stage of adoption.
explain_practitioner: The authors propose a staged evaluation framework for AI in healthcare. They compare it with the trial stages used for drugs and medical devices, noting both similarities and differences. For every stage they offer advice on study design and methods. Their argument is that healthcare is complex and AI performance depends on users and context, so computer based testing alone is insufficient. The key result is a structured, cross disciplinary path for assessing AI implementations in real settings. This gives researchers and engineers a way to plan evidence collection across development and deployment, rather than treating a single technical test as final proof.
